growth_story.headline: Oil lifted Congo's income per person, then the 2014 price crash and heavy debt pulled it back to where it first stood in 1975.
growth_story.arc: Income per person in the Republic of Congo peaked in 1984 and is now 41.8 percent below that peak, about where it first was in 1975. In 1990–1999 it fell 1.9 percent a year, a decade that ended in civil war, which the IMF says cut output outside oil sharply. Growth was nearly flat in 2000–2007, at 0.2 percent a year, then rose to 2.6 in 2008–2015, when debt relief and high oil prices helped growth and the state spent heavily on public works. The oil price shock from 2014 ended that: income per person fell 10.9 percent in 2016 and 7.9 percent in 2017 as spending on public works was cut sharply. Since 2016 it has fallen 3.6 percent a year on average, against 1.5 in the decade before, with another drop of 8.5 percent in 2020 and only a small rise of 0.7 percent in 2025.

threads.title: Civil war in the 1990s
threads.text: Armed conflict in the late 1990s hit the economy outside oil hard and pushed more people into poverty. Income per person fell 1.9 percent a year over 1990–1999.

threads.text: After debt relief in 2010 and with oil prices high, the state spent heavily on public works and day-to-day costs, paid for by oil money and new borrowing. Income per person grew 2.6 percent a year in 2008–2015, the best era since 1990.

threads.text: When oil prices fell from 2014, growth turned sharply negative and the state cut its spending on public works deeply. Income per person fell 10.9 percent in 2016 and 7.9 percent in 2017, and has fallen 3.6 percent a year on average over 2016–2025.

since_last_year.text: In September 2025 the World Bank reported that income per person rose in 2024 for the first time since 2016, while falling oil output showed how fragile growth remains. In March 2026 the IMF said weak public investment, power supply disruptions and slack oil activity had held back growth, and that new unpaid bills had built up. In the data, income per person grew 0.7 percent in 2025, its first rise since 2014.

growth_story.tension: The World Bank says income per person rose in 2024 for the first time since 2016, but the data here show a 0.3 percent fall in 2024 and the first rise in 2025. The IMF also describes the years up to 2014 as a time of faster growth and falling poverty, yet income per person grew only 1.5 percent a year over 2006–2015 and never got back to its 1984 peak.
